goal: Find and name a version of your document
preamble: You've never pressed save in this document, and you never will. Every keystroke you've ever made here is already recorded. You're not about to turn on backups — you're about to learn how to read a timeline that already exists.
generalization: Naming a version is just bookmarking a point on a timeline Docs was recording anyway. It's the same reason you never have to press save: the document isn't a file you're editing, it's a history you're adding to.

steps.intent: Everything about the document as a whole — not the text in it, the document itself — lives under File. That's where a history of the whole document would be.
hints: The leftmost menu, above the toolbar.
Top-left of the window, next to Edit.

steps.intent: Open Version history. The little arrow means there's more underneath — Docs keeps the timeline and the bookmark tools together.
hints: It's in the File menu, in the group about the document's past.
About two-thirds of the way down the File menu.

wrongHints.Make a copy: A copy is a new, separate document. We want this document's own past, not a duplicate of its present.

steps.intent: See version history. This opens the timeline itself — every version Docs has been quietly keeping.
hints: The first option in the submenu that just opened.
Top of the small menu that appeared to the right.

steps.intent: Your turn. Somewhere in what just opened is a way to give the current version a name — so that instead of a timestamp, this moment reads as something you'll recognise later. Find it.
hints: You're labelling a point in time, and the panel is already showing you those points. One of them is this one.
The newest entry at the top of the list — its date is an editable field, not just a label.
